questions.q: What does a Structured Streaming checkpoint store?

options.t: A full copy of the target table, for recovery
options.why: The checkpoint stores progress and state, not a copy of the output.

options.t: The offsets read, the commits made, any state, and the query ID
The code of the query, so it can be restarted without the notebook
options.why: The checkpoint holds progress, not the query's code.

options.t: Only the list of files that failed to load
options.why: It records offsets, commits and state for every micro-batch.

questions.explain: A checkpoint stores offsets (what each micro-batch read), commits (which batches reached the sink, for exactly-once), state (aggregations, joins, deduplication) and the query ID.

questions.q: Two different streaming queries are configured with the same checkpoint location. What does the documentation say?

options.t: It's fine as long as they write different tables
options.why: Each query needs its own checkpoint location; never share one.

options.t: It's recommended, to save storage
options.why: Sharing a checkpoint is never recommended.

options.t: Each query needs its own checkpoint location; never share one
It's required when both read from the same source
options.why: Each query needs its own checkpoint, whatever its source.

questions.explain: Each query needs its own checkpoint location. Two streams writing one Delta table with one checkpoint fail with DELTA_CONCURRENT_TRANSACTION.

questions.q: Which change to a running streaming query is generally safe to make without a new checkpoint?

options.t: Changing the sink from a Delta table to Kafka
options.why: Changing the sink type generally needs a new checkpoint.

options.t: Adding a second source with a union
options.why: Changing the number of sources generally needs a new checkpoint.

options.t: Changing the Auto Loader input path
options.why: Changing Auto Loader paths generally needs a new checkpoint.

options.t: Changing a filter or the trigger interval

questions.explain: Adding or removing filters and changing rate limits and trigger intervals is generally safe; changing sources, Auto Loader paths, stateful operations, state schema or sink type generally needs a new checkpoint.

questions.q: A notebook job on serverless compute uses `.trigger(processingTime='1 minute')`. What does the documentation say?

options.t: Serverless notebooks and jobs support only availableNow and Once triggers
It works, but processingTime costs more on serverless
options.why: Serverless notebooks and jobs support only the availableNow and Once triggers.

options.t: It works only with a pool attached
options.why: Pools are classic compute; serverless supports only availableNow and Once.

options.t: It works if autoscaling is disabled
options.why: The limit is the trigger type, not autoscaling.

questions.explain: Serverless notebooks and jobs support only AvailableNow and Once streaming triggers; for continuous processing on serverless, use a continuous pipeline.

questions.q: Which trigger is not supported on Databricks?

options.t: availableNow
options.why: availableNow is supported and recommended for scheduled incremental jobs.

options.t: processingTime
options.why: processingTime is supported for fixed-interval micro-batches.

options.t: continuous
realTime
options.why: realTime is the trigger for Databricks' real-time mode.

questions.explain: The continuous trigger is not supported on Databricks; micro-batch triggers and real-time mode are.

questions.q: What does a watermark do in a stateful streaming query?

options.t: It guarantees every late record is processed however late it is
options.why: Records later than the threshold might not be processed.

options.t: It bounds state: state older than the threshold behind the latest event time is dropped
It orders records by event time before they are written
options.why: A watermark bounds state; it doesn't sort the output.

options.t: It limits how many files each micro-batch reads
options.why: That is what rate limits do.

questions.explain: The engine tracks the latest event time and drops state older than the threshold. Records within the threshold are always processed; later ones might not be.

questions.q: A team shortens a watermark from 2 hours to 10 minutes. What trade-off have they made?

options.t: Lower latency and less state, but less tolerance for late data
More state and higher latency, but no late data is ever dropped
options.why: That describes lengthening the watermark.

options.t: No effect on state; only the output mode changes
options.why: The watermark directly controls how much state is kept.

options.t: Higher cost, because state is now written twice
options.why: A shorter watermark keeps less state, not more.

questions.explain: A shorter watermark means lower latency and less state but less tolerance for late data; a longer one the reverse.

questions.q: Which output mode rewrites the whole result table on every trigger, and is poor at scale?

options.t: append
options.why: append emits only rows that won't change again.

options.t: update
options.why: update emits only rows changed in this trigger.

options.t: overwrite
options.why: overwrite is a batch write mode, not a streaming output mode.

options.t: complete

questions.explain: complete rewrites the whole result each trigger, for aggregations only; Databricks suggests materialized views instead at scale.

questions.q: Which output mode do stream-stream joins support?

options.t: complete only
options.why: Stream-stream joins support append only.

options.t: append only
update only
options.why: Stream-stream joins support append only.

options.t: any of the three
options.why: Stream-stream joins support append only.

questions.explain: Stream joins support append output mode only.

questions.q: You need to upsert a stream of changes into a Delta table with MERGE. How is that done in Structured Streaming?

options.t: writeStream.format("merge")
options.why: There is no merge sink format; MERGE runs inside foreachBatch.

options.t: writeStream.outputMode("update").toTable(...)
options.why: Update mode emits changed aggregate rows; it doesn't run a MERGE.

options.t: writeStream.foreachBatch(fn), running MERGE inside fn
A streaming read with readChangeFeed set to true
options.why: That reads a table's changes; it doesn't write with MERGE.

questions.explain: foreachBatch runs batch code on each micro-batch and is required for Delta MERGE from a stream.

questions.q: What delivery guarantee does foreachBatch give, and what follows?

options.t: Exactly-once, so the function can append freely
options.why: foreachBatch gives at-least-once writes.

options.t: At-most-once, so failed batches are lost
options.why: Failed batches are retried; the guarantee is at-least-once.

options.t: Exactly-once only when the target has deletion vectors
options.why: Deletion vectors don't change foreachBatch's guarantee.

options.t: At-least-once, so the function should be idempotent, for example a key-based MERGE

questions.explain: foreachBatch provides at-least-once writes; use batch_id or an idempotent operation such as a MERGE on a key so a rerun changes nothing.

questions.q: A silver job should process only rows that changed in a bronze Delta table since its last run. Which feature and read does Databricks recommend?

options.t: Change data feed, read incrementally with spark.readStream and readChangeFeed
DESCRIBE HISTORY, parsed for row values
options.why: History lists operations, not changed rows.

options.t: Time travel to yesterday's version, then a full EXCEPT
options.why: That rereads the whole table; change data feed gives row-level changes.

options.t: VACUUM DRY RUN, to list changed files
options.why: That lists files to delete, not changed rows.

questions.explain: Change data feed records row-level changes between versions; Databricks recommends reading it incrementally with Structured Streaming, which tracks versions for you.

questions.q: Which values can the `_change_type` column of change data feed take?

options.t: insert, update, delete
options.why: Updates appear as update_preimage and update_postimage.

options.t: add, remove, cdc
options.why: Those are transaction log actions, not change types.

options.t: insert, update_preimage, update_postimage, delete
create, merge, vacuum
options.why: Those are operations, not change types.

questions.explain: Each change record carries _change_type (insert, update_preimage, update_postimage, delete), _commit_version and _commit_timestamp.

questions.q: Legacy change data feed was enabled on a table last month. A team asks for the row changes from two months ago. What can they get?

options.t: All changes since the table was created
options.why: Change data feed records changes only after it was enabled.

options.t: Nothing from before it was enabled: it only records changes from then on
The changes, reconstructed from time travel automatically
options.why: Legacy CDF doesn't reconstruct changes from before it was turned on.

options.t: The changes, but only for deletes
options.why: No change types are recorded from before it was enabled.

questions.explain: CDF only records changes after it was enabled; it is not a permanent record.

questions.q: Which path form does Databricks use for ADLS Gen2?

options.t: wasbs://<container>@<account>.blob.core.windows.net/<path>
options.why: That is the legacy Azure Blob driver form; ADLS Gen2 uses abfss.

options.t: dbfs:/mnt/<account>/<container>/<path>
options.why: That is a legacy mount path, not the ADLS Gen2 URI.

options.t: adls://<account>/<container>/<path>
options.why: The scheme is abfss, with the dfs endpoint.

options.t: abfss://<container>@<account>.dfs.core.windows.net/<path>

questions.explain: ADLS Gen2 paths are abfss://<container>@<account>.dfs.core.windows.net/<path>.

questions.q: What is the recommended way for Unity Catalog to read data in an ADLS Gen2 account?

options.t: An account key in a secret scope, set in the cluster's Spark properties
options.why: That is a legacy pattern; Databricks recommends against account keys.

options.t: An Access Connector's managed identity, used in a storage credential and external locations
A SAS token pasted into each notebook
options.why: Tokens in notebooks are neither governed nor recommended.

options.t: Making the container public and reading it anonymously
options.why: That removes access control entirely.

questions.explain: Create an Access Connector (a managed identity), grant it a storage role, and use it in a Unity Catalog storage credential and external locations; no secret rotation is needed.

questions.q: Why does Databricks recommend building silver tables from bronze rather than straight from ingestion?

options.t: Bronze keeps the raw source data, so silver can be rebuilt without asking the source again
Silver tables can't read from cloud storage directly
options.why: They can; the reason is reprocessing and audit from bronze.

options.t: Bronze tables are faster to query than source files
options.why: Speed isn't the reason; bronze is the base for reprocessing and audit.

options.t: Unity Catalog doesn't allow silver tables over external locations
options.why: That isn't a rule; the reason is the reprocessing base bronze provides.

questions.explain: Bronze keeps the source's raw state, appended incrementally, as the base for reprocessing and audit. Build silver from bronze, mostly with streaming reads of append-only bronze.

questions.q: Which provenance column does Databricks suggest adding in bronze when loading files with Auto Loader?

options.t: _change_type
options.why: That is a change data feed column, not provenance for loaded files.

options.t: _commit_version
options.why: That is a change data feed column.

options.t: _rescued_data
options.why: That holds values that don't fit the schema, not provenance.

options.t: The source file name, from _metadata.file_name

questions.explain: Bronze adds provenance metadata such as the source file name (_metadata.file_name with Auto Loader) and the load time.

questions.q: In which mode does Databricks run Structured Streaming by default, and what latency does it target?

options.t: Real-time mode, with latency of a few milliseconds
options.why: Real-time mode is for sub-second operational workloads; the default is micro-batch.

options.t: Micro-batch mode, with latency of seconds to minutes
Continuous mode, with sub-millisecond latency
options.why: Continuous mode isn't supported on Databricks.

options.t: Batch mode, run once a day
options.why: Structured Streaming runs incrementally; the default is micro-batch mode.

questions.explain: Databricks runs Structured Streaming in micro-batch mode by default (seconds to minutes, for ETL and analytics), or in real-time mode for sub-second operational workloads.

questions.q: A stream reads a bronze Delta table. Someone runs RESTORE on that table to an older version. What can happen downstream?

options.t: Nothing: RESTORE is a metadata-only operation
options.why: RESTORE is a data-changing operation that re-adds files.

options.t: The stream rewinds to the restored version automatically
options.why: The stream doesn't rewind; it sees the restored files as new data.

options.t: The stream sees the restored files as new data and can write duplicates
The stream stops permanently and must be dropped
options.why: The risk is duplicates, not a permanent stop.

questions.explain: RESTORE is a data-changing operation (dataChange=true), so a stream reading the table sees it as new data and can produce duplicates downstream.

questions.q: A stream writes to a Delta table with toTable, without foreachBatch. It fails and restarts. Why doesn't it write the last micro-batch twice?

options.t: The Delta sink records each batch with a transaction identifier in the log and skips batches already committed
The checkpoint's commits record which batches reached the sink
Delta tables reject duplicate rows by default
options.why: Primary keys are informational; Delta doesn't reject duplicate rows.

options.t: Auto Loader deletes the source files after each batch
options.why: Auto Loader doesn't delete source files.

options.t: The stream always starts from the beginning after a failure
options.why: It resumes from its checkpoint.

questions.explain: The checkpoint's commits record which batches reached the sink, and the Delta sink records an application ID and version (a txn action) atomically with each batch, skipping a batch already committed.
